item.title: Iranian women are facing not just lashings, but "honor killings"
item.description:
Helia Fattahi told her parents she was pregnant. She was not married. They allegedly killed her.
Iranian police arrested both parents after the killing on Nov. 21 in Sanandaj, a city in the mountains of western Iran. According to local media, they confessed, citing the shame they believed their daughter had brought upon the family.
The provincial police chief, however, described the motive in more prosaic terms, calling it "family disputes," and the parents have not been charged with any crimes.
Two days later, in the holy city of Qom, another Iranian woman was violently punished for a different act of defiance.
Parastoo Ahmadi, a celebrated singer, and four members of her production team each received 74 lashes over a concert she had performed nearly two years earlier without wearing a headscarf.
Iranian singer Parastoo Ahmadi was lashed 74 times Monday by Iranian authorities for "outraging public decency" by singing without a hijab in a 2024 concert.
One woman had defied the conventions of her family. The other had defied the laws of the state.
Both cases, along with a spate of killings of young women across Iran in recent weeks, illuminate the sharp and still fragile limits to the modest freedoms Iranian women have secured since a popular uprising shook the Islamic Republic four years ago.
At the heart of that struggle are questions about who gets to decide how Iranian women live — what they wear, whom they love, and whether they can marry who they choose.
The protests first erupted in 2022 after Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman, died in police custody after being arrested for wearing her headscarf improperly. Her family told CBS News she was tortured in custody.
Women discarded their hair coverings, challenged the authority of Iran's morality police, and asserted freedoms that...

item.title: Trump says he's giving Iran "a chance to be smart"
item.description:
What to know about the Iran war today: President Trump said Thursday that victory in the war with Iran would be achieved "whenever I want it," and that he is giving the Islamic Republic regime "a chance to be smart," though he said he doubts they will take it. Mr. Trump also downplayed the importance of Russia and China's intelligence sharing with Iran after multiple reports that Tehran's allies have helped it target U.S. military assets in the Middle East.Iran denied on Thursday being behind a drone attack on a Kuwaiti military facility that killed two Italian nationals. The head of the European Commission called for more international pressure on Iran over the incident.
New Updates
8:21 AM
Iran claims another oil tanker has struck a sea mine near the Strait of Hormuz
Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed yet another oil tanker was on fire Friday after hitting a sea mine near the Strait of Hormuz. In a statement carried by Iranian state TV network IRIB, the IRGC Navy's Public Relations Office said the unidentified vessel hit the mine while attempting to transit the strait via an "unauthorized route."
Iran uses the term to refer to southern shipping lanes through the waterway that the U.S. military insists are safe and mine-free, but Tehran has repeatedly warned vessels to avoid.
The latest claim was not immediately confirmed by independent maritime agencies. The IRGC said a second tanker accompanying the vessel was forced to turn back.

item.title: Murder suspect crashes into elephant while fleeing police
item.description:
A Sri Lankan man suspected of fatally stabbing a woman was arrested on Friday after he crashed his scooter into a wild elephant as he attempted to escape, police said.
The 49-year-old man is accused of stabbing the woman in her home in the northern district of Anuradhapura, a police official told AFP.
However, his attempted escape ended when his scooter crashed into the elephant as it emerged from the jungle onto the road a short distance away, the official said.
Witnesses told police the elephant appeared to be unharmed and retreated back into the jungle.
The man was arrested and was receiving treatment for unspecified injuries under armed guard in hospital. Police also said they had recovered the suspected murder weapon.
Encounters between humans and elephants are relatively common in Sri Lanka, where expanding settlements and farms often overlap with animal habitats.
The island recorded about 400 elephant and 150 human deaths annually over the past five years, according to official figures.
Sri Lanka is home to an estimated 7,000 wild elephants and considers the animals a national treasure that are protected by law.
However, residents in remote villages sometimes attack elephants that destroy their crops.
According to the World Wildlife Fund, "the Sri Lanka elephant is protected under the Sri Lankan law and killing one carries the death penalty."
Conservationists and veterinarians have previously warned that plastic waste in a landfill in eastern Sri Lanka was killing elephants in the region. In 2020, drone footage captured more than a dozen hungry elephants scouring for food in the landfill.
Elephants in the country are also sometimes injured or killed by trains. Last year, a Sri Lankan express train killed an elephant and was derailed. The incident happened three months after seven elephants were fatally struck on the same route, marking the country's worst wildlife railway accident.

item.title: U.S. opens hotline for tips about cartels, angering Mexico
item.description:
Mexico's president has blasted the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration after it set up anonymous tip lines in the country, accusing American officials of "interference" and not doing enough to fight fentanyl and corruption inside their own borders.
President Claudia Sheinbaum, in harsh comments Thursday, read excerpts from a new investigation by The Associated Press revealing how the DEA allowed at least 1.4 million counterfeit fentanyl pills to go unseized as it spent eight months tracking a drug trafficking ring flooding the Southwest with deadly drugs.
"The DEA has plenty of work to do in its own country. A lot," Sheinbaum said, pointing to the AP report. "The first thing it should do is investigate corruption in the United States linked to organized crime, or what they call terrorist groups."
"It's clearly an act of interference," Sheinbaum added.
Imagine, she mused, if Mexico "opened a WhatsApp service for reporting corruption in the United States. How would the U.S. government view that?"
Sheinbaum's angry response comes less than 24 hours after DEA Administrator Terry Cole announced the tip lines on his X account, encouraging Mexicans to denounce members of criminal networks in Sinaloa state, the corrupt officials who support them and people who launder money to finance narcoterrorism.
"Your information matters. Your identity and your safety matter," Cole said, specifying that tips submitted via Signal, WhatsApp and email would be handled confidentially.
U.S. steps up pressure on Mexico
The United States has stepped up pressure on Mexico to fight the cartels and has even offered to deploy troops on Mexican soil, something Sheinbaum has ruled out while maintaining that there will be security cooperation with Washington, "but without subordination."

item.title: Germany arrests 2 Iraqis allegedly tied to Iran-linked terror group
item.description:
Berlin — German authorities on Thursday arrested two Iraqi men on suspicion of terrorism. The suspects are alleged to be members of an Iran-linked terrorist organization that is said to have targeted U.S., Israeli and Jewish institutions in Europe.
The men, who were arrested in Cologne and Heidelberg by the Federal Criminal Police Office, are Iraqi nationals Mostafa Al-R. and Ameer J., according to the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office.
The investigation centers on alleged links to Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya, a shadowy group that emerged to claim a series of sabotage, arson and violent attacks targeting Jewish institutions in Europe not long after the start of the U.S. war with Iran. The U.S. government has labeled HAYI a front for Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the Iran-backed militia Kataib Hezbollah in Iraq. Britain has designated HAYI as a terrorist organization.
According to investigators, Mostafa Al-R. is alleged to have maintained contact with Mohammad Al-Saadi, who is currently facing criminal charges in the United States. Al-Saadi is considered a central figure within the alleged terrorist network.
As early as late 2025, Al-Saadi, Mostafa Al-R. and other individuals allegedly founded an independent group whose goal was to carry out terrorist attacks in Germany and other European countries, according to prosecutors. Ameer J. is also a member of this group, they said.
The group planned to target synagogues in Cologne and another European city, prosecutors alleged, saying unknown perpetrators traveled to the locations in March 2026 on behalf of the organization. The plans were not implemented for unknown reasons.
HAYI is also linked to attacks on Jewish institutions in the United Kingdom, France, Belgium and the Netherlands, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution said.
The suspects are accused of membership in a domestic terrorist organization under Section 129a of Germany's Criminal Code. ...

item.title: Could the Black Sea pull the U.S. into war in Europe?
item.description:
Constanța, Romania – Out on the Black Sea, the Romanian Navy is always on the lookout for the deadly debris of a war it isn't fighting.
It's a front of the Russia-Ukraine war that most people rarely see. It runs right up to NATO's doorstep and sometimes crosses into its waters — threatening to pull the alliance, and therefore the United States, into the war.
Incidents involving drones, mines and commercial ships are surging in the Black Sea, NATO military spokesperson Colonel Martin O'Donnell told CBS News.
"In 2025, for example, we saw fewer than 50 incidents in the Black Sea. This year alone, we're talking four to five hundred," he said.
American NATO spokesperson Martin O'Donnell told CBS News in November 2026 that the Black Sea may be "more important" than the Strait of Hormuz.
CBS News
The roughly tenfold increase threatens a major artery of global grain and fuel shipments and has made the waterway deadlier than the Strait of Hormuz, a flashpoint in the U.S.-Iran war, with both sides trying to enforce blockades on the chokepoint to exert economic pressure on the other.
Twenty-five sailors have been killed in the strait this year, according to the International Maritime Organization, while at least 40 have been killed in the Black Sea in the same period, according to the International Transport Workers' Federation.
"I would say the Black Sea is just as important, and then depending on who you talk to, some might argue could perhaps even be more important … in terms of global trade," said O'Donnell.
Any imbalance in the flow of fuel and food "can have global implications that can impact America just as much as it can any of the nations here," he said.
